Regardless of the criticism of Arsenal’s dour style of play, it earnt them the EPL title and a narrow defeat in an epic Champions League decider.

There are different ways to play the beautiful game and some of them can be quite ugly. Arsenal, for instance, became champions of England last month by perfecting a defensiveness so uncaring about the higher aesthetics of the game that neutral fans complained of migraines and spontaneous nosebleeds.

Worse, Arsenal’s indifference to actually possessing the ball incentivised their physicality and the necessity of scoring from dead balls – free kicks and corners. So, in turn, they were incentivised to milk these with a mix of theatricality, negative positioning and the obnoxious badgering of refs.

Comparing Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta with Ange Postecoglou is akin to juxtaposing Nurse Ratched and Randle McMurphy. They are philosophical opposites, with Postecoglou infamously stressing “purposeful” possession above all else. Get the ball, hold on to it and score more than the other mob. We’re painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel here, boys, not carrying the drip trays. Aussie Ange made few concessions to his gallantry and as a result was either celebrated as a daring aesthete or as soccer’s Chauncey Gardiner.

Among fans, there has always been some tension between aesthetes and instrumentalists. Rarely, however, is one a fundamentalist about either: if the unattractive style of your new manager is yielding results, perhaps some concessions can be made.

And lord knows that Arteta, considered by many as an assassin of beauty, brought a league title to North London for the first time in 22 years. His job, after all, is not to uphold our ideas of athletic grace but simply to win. And he has.

Last weekend, Arsenal also played in the Champions League final in Budapest. They did so against the reigning European champions, Paris Saint-Germain, a team revered by neutrals for their gorgeousness. Fast, fluent, inventive, ceaselessly attacking – here, it seemed, was a classic encounter of good and evil; righteousness and cynicism.

If only it were so simple.

Still, these were high stakes for Arteta’s team and those who follow them. It is an extraordinary achievement to win both your domestic league and the Champions League in the same season – unless you’re PSG, of course, who enjoy the infinite riches of Qatari ownership and who play in a league so poor you can often field reserve squads to better rest your superstars.

Just seven British clubs have won the European title, and of them only Chelsea has come from London. Arsenal had appeared in just one European Cup/Champions League final before, precisely 20 years ago, and so my point is hopefully obvious: an Arsenal double would likely have given Mick Jagger a cardiac arrest and finally ended the Rolling Stones in a way heroin or the 1980s never could.

Arsenal were, as feared, defensively implacable and indifferent about possession. PSG recorded 837 completed passes to Arsenal’s 199, while possession split 75/25 in favour of the Parisians (the “Parisians” owned by a petrostate and managed by a Spaniard).

But if this small statistical insight suggests to you PSG’s domination, you’d be wrong. Arsenal’s defending was so fanatical, so deep and disciplined, that precious little of PSG’s possession translated into meaningful attacks. With the exception of a few fast breaks, Paris could only turn their lion’s share of the ball into ineffectual prodding.

Arsenal, then, had allowed them just as much of the ball as they wanted them to have. We had here a thrilling contest of styles: one made more delicious early on when a lucky rebounding deflection allowed Arsenal striker Kai Havertz to run towards goal five minutes into the game and smash past the PSG keeper from an acute angle. This early goal strengthened Arsenal’s hand – they’d now fortuitously acquitted the chore of scoring, and could now double-down on their great skill: negating beauty. PSG’s famed offensive genius would have to be very good indeed to breach the Great Red Wall of Budapest.

“Ugliness” is a measure of the freedom of how coaches decide to direct their players. That freedom is more important to me than how the sport’s administrators view the commercial attractiveness of its “product”.

It is at this point that the neutral fan shakes their fist and curses the vandals. But for all my jesting about Arsenal’s ugliness, the engagement of these two very different teams created a thrilling spectacle. Not of beauty, perhaps, but the drama of two excellent sides of different but equally potent abilities meeting for this grand trophy.

We would not get a thrilling 5-4 game, as we did in the first leg of the semi-final between PSG and Bayern Munich; but nor would we get the sour spectacle of last year’s final when Paris embarrassed Inter Milan 5-0. There are shades to soccer and still something of a spectrum of styles, and last weekend we enjoyed their tense, self-cancelling combination.

This was a wonderfully dramatic final and I was grateful for its defining question: was Arsenal defensively good enough to absorb the attacking genius of Paris? Yes and no came the answer, and the game ended after regulation time at 1-1 – a fair stalemate.

For the first time in 10 years, a Champions League final went to extra-time – and during a sweltering European summer and a humid Hungarian night. As can often happen in extra-time, the multitude of heavy, bruised and cramping legs can humiliate the talents of their owners, and on this night the additional 30 minutes were marked by caution and the sloppiness of fatigue. If Arsenal often play cautiously, the change of mentality was at least conspicuous in PSG: they understood that the likelihood of scoring from offensive adventures in extra-time was lower than the likelihood of calamitously conceding something while trying.

So, after two hours of play, and the teams still deadlocked on one goal each, we went to that cruel lottery, the penalty shootout. Of the 10 penalty kicks taken, two players performed the stuttering run-up and pause before striking so as to encourage the goalkeeper’s intention. Both of these players were from Arsenal; both missed. It’s a small sample size, but like the AFL veterans displeased with the modern habit of snapping set kicks, I have a powerful aversion to this style of penalty kick.

The stutter and pause is meant to reveal the goalkeeper’s direction – typically, the keeper has chosen pre-emptively where to dive because the distance between them and the ball is so small as to make acting on reflex alone impractical. But if we remove the psychological pressure, then the penalty kick itself is designed to overwhelmingly favour the kicker. It shouldn’t require the cute hiccupping we saw from Gabriel Magalhães and Eberechi Eze to ostensibly milk additional advantage from something already advantageous.

Liverpool legend and Champions League trophy holder Steven Gerrard thought the same: “Think about the magnitude of the game, the stadium, the atmosphere, it’s hard enough without any of that nonsense,” he said after the game. “Put your foot through it, back your technique.”

Indeed. Now here’s former England international Owen Hargreaves: “I’ve never been a big fan of that run-up; I think it puts you under pressure,” he said. “I prefer players picking their corner and smashing it in. If you stutter, you can put a bit of doubt in your own mind if the goalkeeper doesn’t move.”

Precisely – and the goalkeeper didn’t move, thus perversely rendering the attempt to find advantage a terrible disadvantage as one scrambles to improvise a shot in a fraction of a second. You will have also relinquished the power that comes from a full, fluent run-up to the kick.

Here ends my armchair TED Talk.

As it was, Arsenal were “ugly” enough to negate the octane talents of PSG – and I commend them. As I commend the German referee, Daniel Siebert. He was not one to be bullied or bamboozled, and he respected the clock as much as the flow of the game when he waved “play on” after several pratfalls designed to attract free kicks. The wisdom of a referee can be seen just as often in the moments that his whistle doesn’t blow.

Anyway: on this humid night, Arsenal lost on penalties 3-4. A terrible way to lose, or even to win, but so it goes. This lottery, this acid-bath for the nerves, is how we resolve deadlocks in the beautiful game.

The aesthete might celebrate Arsenal’s loss as a moral victory, but Arsenal’s style worked. Champions of England, they came within a whisker of defeating a super-team who have the luxury of resting their stars during the domestic season. Their advantages are untold and Arsenal neutered them.

It also remains a virtue of the world game that success might be found with a variety of tactics and that managers and coaches still retain some agency to enact them. Less so in the AFL, where in the past few years the game’s administration has imposed many substantial rule changes to fundamentally alter how the game is played.

Sensitive to complaints that Australian Rules had become unwatchable – a dull smudge of rolling scrums and hyper-congestion – the AFL began solving the problem by dictate.

The 6-6-6 rule of a few years ago, mandating the formation of teams across three sectors of the ground before the resumption of play, was significant. So too the authorised leniency of kick-outs from the goal square after a behind was scored. These rules were introduced to dissolve congestion; to make the game more fluent. So too the stand rule, now enforced with eye-watering severity, and this year’s changes to ball-outs between the 50 metre arcs.

In all cases, the rule changes were made to alter a “product”, not a sport, and to make that product more palatable – faster, more fluent. On that count, it has worked. But I maintain the game’s style and tactics should evolve organically – that is, by players and coaches and not the hyperreactive administrators of a commercial behemoth.

There is a loss of agency when the AFL embarks upon its vainglorious mission to make more perfect “the perfect sport” – as there is a collapsing of distinctions between how teams play the game.

“Ugliness” is a measure of the freedom of how coaches decide to direct their players. That freedom is more important to me than how the sport’s administrators view the commercial attractiveness of its “product”. A variety of tactics should flourish – and be allowed to prevail or perish as per things messier, richer and more organic than the boardroom of the AFL.

But for some years now, we have had the heavy thumb of the AFL pressed upon our game. The footy may have suddenly become faster and less congested but at the immediate cost of clubs relinquishing agency and tactical character to the blithe administrators.

So, let me here sympathise with Arsenal’s “ugliness” – for it speaks to freedom and the richness that follows from antagonistic philosophies meeting each other.

How the game is played should be determined by those playing it and not the PR agents, lawyers and MBAs rewriting the game’s rules.

Martin McKenzie-Murray is The Saturday Paper’s associate editor.
